what_it_does: Modern graphics processors are increasingly built by stitching several smaller chips (called modules) together on a shared circuit board or interposer, rather than making one giant chip. The wires that connect these modules carry limited bandwidth, and when one module needs data sitting in another module's memory, it must travel a long, congested path. NearFetch is a routing trick that checks whether any chip along that path already has a cached copy of the requested data; if so, it fetches from that nearby chip instead of going all the way to the far memory. This avoids wasting the precious inter-module link capacity and speeds up workloads that share a lot of data across modules. The paper also introduces a new measurement called Inter-Module Bandwidth per Access to quantify how much of that shared link is being wasted on long-haul fetches.
